topics.title: Diversity of living things
topics.summary: What all living things do; classifying animals, plants, fungi and bacteria.

steps.text: Touch a makahiya leaf. It folds up! What else shows that something is alive?
All living things need food, water and air, grow, respond to changes around them, and reproduce. A car moves, but cannot grow or reproduce, so it is not alive.
Your turn: Which shows that a kitten is living?

interact.prompt: Which shows that a kitten is living?
interact.explain: Growing is a sign of life.

steps.text: A whale lives in the sea like a fish. A bat flies like a bird. Are they fish and birds?

We group animals by their features. Mammals have fur and feed their young milk, so whales and bats are mammals. Birds have feathers; fish have gills; reptiles have dry scales; amphibians have moist skin; insects have six legs.
Your turn: Which animal group does it belong to?

interact.prompt: Which animal group does it belong to?
interact.explain: A horse is a mammal: it has hair or fur and feeds its young on milk.

steps.text: Look under a fern leaf. You may see tiny brown dots. A gumamela has big red flowers.
Flowering plants make flowers, then fruits with seeds. Non-flowering plants do not: ferns and mosses make spores, and pine trees make seeds in cones.
Your turn: Is it a flowering or a non-flowering plant?

interact.prompt: Is it a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
interact.explain: A coconut tree has small flowers that grow into coconuts.

steps.text: Seal a slice of damp bread in a clear plastic bag and leave it somewhere warm for a few days. Fuzzy mould grows on it. Do not open, touch or sniff it; throw it away still sealed.

Mould, mushrooms and yeast are fungi. They cannot make their own food; they feed on what they grow on and make spores. Bacteria are tiny living things seen only with a microscope. Some are harmful, some helpful.
Your turn: Which shows that some bacteria are helpful?

interact.prompt: Which shows that some bacteria are helpful?
interact.explain: Some bacteria turn milk into yogurt. Others cause disease or spoil food.

topics.title: Materials
topics.summary: Properties of materials and why we choose them.

steps.text: Bend a rubber band, a plastic ruler and a stick. Drop a cloth and a plastic cup onto a soft mat. (Glass would break and could cut you.)
Materials differ in strength, hardness, flexibility, whether they are waterproof, whether light passes through, and whether they float.
Your turn: A material you can see clearly through is…

interact.prompt: A material you can see clearly through is…
interact.explain: Transparent materials, like clear glass, let light through.

steps.text: Why is a pot metal but its handle plastic? Why is a window glass?
We choose a material because of its properties. Metal lets heat through to cook food; plastic does not, so it keeps our hands safe. Glass is transparent, so light comes in.
Your turn: Why are many bridges made of steel?

interact.prompt: Why are many bridges made of steel?
choices: Steel is as light as paper.
interact.explain: Steel is strong enough to hold up heavy cars and trucks.

topics.title: Life cycles
topics.summary: How animals and plants grow and reproduce.

steps.text: A caterpillar eats and grows, then hangs still as a pupa. Weeks later, a butterfly comes out!

Some animals have 4 stages: egg, larva, pupa, adult (butterfly, mosquito). Others have 3: egg, young, adult (chicken, cockroach). A frog changes from a tadpole in water to an adult that can live on land.
Your turn: In the life cycle of a frog, what comes just before "egg"?

interact.prompt: In the life cycle of a frog, what comes just before "egg"?

visual.label: the life cycle of a frog

interact.explain: The life cycle of a frog: egg → tadpole → tadpole with legs → young frog (froglet) → adult frog, and then it starts again. The adult frog lays eggs in water, and the cycle starts again.

steps.text: Look for still water in old cans and tyres around your home. Tiny wriggling larvae may be mosquitoes.
Mosquito larvae live in still water. Emptying containers stops mosquitoes from breeding, which helps prevent dengue.
Your turn: A caterpillar sheds its skin as it grows. Why?

interact.prompt: A caterpillar sheds its skin as it grows. Why?
choices: Its skin cannot stretch, so it grows a bigger one.
interact.answer: Its skin cannot stretch, so it grows a bigger one.
interact.explain: Insects moult: they shed their old skin to grow bigger.

steps.text: Plant a mung bean (monggo) seed in wet cotton. Watch it grow day by day.
A seed germinates into a seedling, grows into an adult plant, makes flowers, and the flowers become fruits with seeds. The seeds start the cycle again.
Your turn: In the life cycle of a flowering plant, what comes just before "seed"?

interact.prompt: In the life cycle of a flowering plant, what comes just before "seed"?

visual.label: the life cycle of a flowering plant

interact.explain: The life cycle of a flowering plant: seed → seedling → adult plant → flower → fruit with seeds, and then it starts again. The seeds in the fruit grow into new plants, and the cycle starts again.

topics.title: Plant and body systems
topics.summary: Plant parts and their jobs; the digestive system.

steps.text: Put a celery stalk in coloured water. After a day, the colour reaches the leaves.
Roots hold the plant and take in water and mineral salts. The stem holds the plant up and carries water and food. Leaves make food. Flowers become fruits, which protect the seeds.
Your turn: A plant's stem is cut through. What happens to the leaves after a while?

interact.prompt: A plant's stem is cut through. What happens to the leaves after a while?
choices: They droop because they get no water.
interact.answer: They droop because they get no water.
interact.explain: The stem carries water. Without it, the leaves droop and dry up.

steps.text: Chew a piece of bread for a long time. It starts to taste sweet: digestion has begun in your mouth.
Food goes from the mouth, down the gullet, to the stomach, then the small intestine and the large intestine.

visual.text: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
visual.label: mouth → gullet → stomach → small intestine → large intestine

steps.text: Digestion breaks food into tiny pieces. In the small intestine, digested food passes into the blood. The large intestine takes in water, and what is left leaves the body.
Your turn: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach?

interact.prompt: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
interact.explain: The gullet carries food down to the stomach. The windpipe carries air.

topics.title: Magnets
topics.summary: Magnetic materials; poles that attract and repel.

steps.text: Test a steel paper clip, an aluminium can and a copper wire with a magnet. All three are metals. Which ones stick?
Magnets attract iron and steel. Not every metal is magnetic: aluminium, copper and gold are not attracted.
Your turn: Will a magnet attract it?

interact.explain: A steel safety pin is attracted by a magnet: it is made of iron or steel.

steps.text: Push the N poles of two magnets together. You can feel them push apart! Now turn one around.
Every magnet has a north (N) and a south (S) pole. Like poles repel. Unlike poles attract. Only a magnet can repel another magnet.

visual.text: N → ← S attract · N ← → N repel
visual.label: N → ← S attract · N ← → N repel

steps.text: Your turn: Two bar magnets are placed end to end, as shown. What will they do?

interact.prompt: Two bar magnets are placed end to end, as shown. What will they do?
interact.explain: The ends facing each other are S and S. Like poles repel.

topics.title: Think like a scientist
topics.summary: Read an experiment and its results.

steps.text: Scientists ask a question, then test it. For example: does light help plants grow? Give 4 plants different hours of light, and measure them.
In a fair test, we change one thing and measure what happens. We write the results in a table so we can compare them.
Your turn: What did Ben change in this experiment?

interact.prompt: What did Ben change in this experiment?

items.title: Dissolving sugar
items.text: Ben stirred 1 spoon of sugar into each of 4 cups of water at different temperatures. Ben timed how long the sugar took to dissolve.

choices: the time the sugar took to dissolve
interact.explain: Only the temperature of the water was different for each one, so that is what was changed.
